finding.summary: The PRD defines password-only login, trusts a client-supplied X-Tenant header for tenancy, and mandates non-expiring sessions — together enabling credential attacks, trivial cross-tenant access, and permanent session theft.

claims.text: Password-only authentication is specified with no rate limiting, MFA, lockout, or hashing requirements, leaving login exposed to brute force and credential stuffing.

Tenancy is derived from the client-controlled X-Tenant header on every request, with no requirement to validate it against the authenticated user's authorized tenants, enabling cross-tenant data access.
Sessions never expire, so any stolen session token grants permanent access with no revocation or rotation requirement.
The PRD omits transport security, cookie attributes, CSRF protection, and audit logging requirements.

recommendations: Derive tenant context server-side from the authenticated session; validate any X-Tenant hint against the user's tenant membership and reject mismatches.
Require session expiration (idle and absolute timeouts), token rotation after login/privilege change, and explicit revocation support.
Add rate limiting, lockout/backoff, optional MFA, a password policy, and modern password hashing (Argon2id/bcrypt).
Mandate TLS-only transport and secure cookie attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) plus CSRF protection.
Require audit logging of authentication events and tenant-scoped data access, and define a secure password-reset flow.
questions: Is the X-Tenant header intended only as a hint, with tenant membership enforced against server-side session data?
What threat model drove the 'sessions never expire' requirement — is a long-lived refresh-token pattern with short-lived access tokens acceptable instead?
Are MFA, rate limiting, and lockout out of scope, or simply not yet specified in this PRD?
How will cross-tenant access attempts and authentication failures be logged and alerted on?
